implementation_notes: The stdlib `dataclasses.dataclass` decorator generates `__init__`, a field-by-field `__eq__` (identical type required) and - with `frozen=True, eq=True` - `__hash__`, while assigning to a frozen field raises `FrozenInstanceError`; `slots=True` (3.10+) drops the per-instance `__dict__`, and `__post_init__` (with `object.__setattr__`) is where validation and normalisation happen. That replaces the hand-written class with `__slots__`, `__eq__` and `__hash__`; the classic form is still needed when attribute names must be dynamic or when instances must stay mutable but comparable.
pitfalls: `frozen=True` only blocks assignment to declared fields: a mutable field (list, dict, object) can still be mutated in place, and `__hash__` then changes with it.
The generated `__eq__` requires both operands to be the same class and compares fields in order; a subclass instance never compares equal to its base.
Frozen instances hash by field values, so they must not contain mutable fields while used as dict keys; `slots=True` also rejects attributes that are not declared fields.

variants.name: attrs frozen class
variants.implementation_notes: *attrs* provides the same recipe with more machinery: `@attrs.frozen` (or `@attr.s(frozen=True, slots=True)`) generates `__init__`, `__eq__` and `__hash__`, slotted classes by default, and lets validators and converters be attached to each attribute so validation runs during initialisation; `attrs.evolve` performs the copy-with-changes update. It is the pre-3.7 route and remains justified when validation or coercion belongs to the attribute definitions themselves; dataclasses need no dependency and less magic.
pitfalls: Like dataclasses, `attrs.frozen` is shallow: nested mutables stay mutable, and `attrs.asdict()` only deep-copies when `recurse=True`.
Converters change the stored value relative to the argument, so the public attribute may differ from what the caller passed - document the normalisation.
Frozen classes are hashed by field values, so a non-hashable or mutable field breaks hashing at first use.
